slide.title: Fine-Tune in Thirty Lines
slide.body: A stack of transformer blocks with a small teal head on top, feeding four boxes: World · Sports · Business · Sci/Tech. Small tag: Deep Learning and Neural Networks · Lesson 13.

scenes.on_screen_text: From dataset to model, thirty lines
scenes.voiceover: In lesson ten, you gave a pretrained image network a new head, and taught it bean diseases. The same idea works for text. With Hugging Face, the whole process, from raw dataset to evaluated model, fits in about thirty lines.

slide.title: Part 1: Dataset
slide.body: load_dataset from the Hub → DatasetDict with train and test · .shuffle(seed).select(range(n)) for a subset · train_test_split for validation

scenes.voiceover: Fine-tuning a transformer for classification has five parts. First, the dataset. The datasets library loads public data from the Hub with its splits. You can take a shuffled subset, and split off a validation set from the training data.

slide.title: Part 2: Tokenise in batches
slide.body:
ds.map(tokenize, batched=True)   # truncate to max_length
DataCollatorWithPadding(tok)      # pad per batch

scenes.voiceover: Second, tokenisation in batches. The map method runs the tokenizer on many rows at once, and caches the result. Truncate to a maximum length that fits most texts. Padding happens later, per batch, with a data collator, which is faster.

slide.title: Part 3: Model
slide.body:
AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name, num_labels=4)
# warning: some weights newly initialized → expected

scenes.voiceover: Third, the model. The auto class for sequence classification loads the pretrained encoder and adds a new, random classification head. A warning that some weights are newly initialised is expected.

slide.title: Parts 4 and 5: Arguments and Trainer
slide.body: TrainingArguments: lr · batch size · epochs · weight decay · eval and save strategy (names change by version) · Trainer: the L05 loop, devices, evaluation, checkpoints · compute_metrics: accuracy, F1

scenes.voiceover: Fourth, the training arguments. They hold the learning rate, batch size, epochs, weight decay, and when to evaluate and save. Parameter names change between versions, so check them against your installed library. Fifth, the Trainer runs the loop from lesson five for you, and a metrics function reports accuracy and F1.

slide.title: Images vs text fine-tuning
slide.body: L10 ResNet: freeze, then unfreeze top block. L13 small transformer: fine-tune all layers, lr about 2e-5 to 5e-5, a few epochs.

scenes.voiceover: Unlike lesson ten, you usually fine-tune all layers of a small transformer, with a small learning rate, often around two to five times ten to the minus five, for a few epochs.

scenes.stock_query: translator working with books and laptop
scenes.on_screen_text: Learn the house style, not the language
scenes.voiceover: Think of an experienced translator who joins a new publishing house. They do not relearn the language. They spend a few days learning the house style. Fine-tuning is those few days. Small, careful adjustments to skills that are already there.

scenes.stock_query: person reading news headlines on tablet
scenes.voiceover: Joaquín is a data scientist at a news aggregator in Rosario, Argentina. He wants to sort English headlines into four topics. World, Sports, Business, and Science and Technology. He prototypes with AG News, a public topic dataset.

screen_steps: Show the AG News and distilbert-base-uncased Hub pages (licence sections)
scenes.on_screen_text: Small subsets for free GPU time
scenes.voiceover: In Colab, he loads the dataset and takes small subsets, so training fits in free GPU time. Four thousand training examples, with twenty percent split off for validation, and two thousand test examples.

screen_steps: Run: tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name); enc = lambda b: tok(b["text"], truncation=True, max_length=128)
Run: train, test = train.map(enc, batched=True), test.map(enc, batched=True)
Run: model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name, num_labels=4); point to the 'newly initialized' warning
scenes.voiceover: He loads the DistilBERT tokenizer, tokenises both splits with map, truncating at one hundred and twenty-eight tokens, and creates the model with four labels.

screen_steps: Run the metrics cell: accuracy_score and f1_score(average="macro")

Run the TrainingArguments cell: learning_rate=3e-5, num_train_epochs=2, per_device_train_batch_size=32, weight_decay=0.01, eval_strategy="epoch", save_strategy="epoch", load_best_model_at_end=True, seed=42, report_to="none"
scenes.on_screen_text: Check argument names for your version
scenes.voiceover: Next, a metrics function for accuracy and macro F1. Then the training arguments. A learning rate of three times ten to the minus five, two epochs, batches of thirty-two, evaluation and saving every epoch, and keep the best model at the end.

screen_steps: Run: trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train["train"], eval_dataset=train["test"], data_collator=DataCollatorWithPadding(tok), compute_metrics=metrics)
Run: trainer.train() and show the per-epoch validation metrics
scenes.voiceover: He builds the Trainer with the validation split as the evaluation set, and a data collator for padding. He trains, and then evaluates the test subset only once, at the end. He reports the accuracy and F1 he measured, and notes the subset sizes, because results on four thousand examples are not comparable with published results on the full dataset.

scenes.on_screen_text: Never choose checkpoints on the test set
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is passing the test split as the evaluation set, with keep best model switched on. The Trainer then picks the checkpoint that is best on the test set, and the test score is too optimistic.

slide.title: Keep evaluation honest
slide.body: eval_dataset = validation split · test split: evaluate once at the end · unexpected keyword argument? Check TrainingArguments names for your version

scenes.voiceover: Use a validation split during training, and touch the test split once. And if you copy arguments from an old tutorial, you may get an unexpected keyword error. Check the names for your version.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. datasets → map(batched=True) → data collator. 2. New head on a pretrained encoder; fine-tune all layers, small lr. 3. Validate to choose, test once; check argument names.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, load data with the datasets library, tokenise in batches with map, and pad per batch with a data collator. Second, the sequence classification model adds a new head to a pretrained encoder. Fine-tune all layers with a small learning rate for a few epochs. Third, choose checkpoints on a validation split, evaluate the test split once, and check argument names against your installed version.

Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will fine-tune a small pretrained model on a subset of AG News, and report accuracy and F1 on the test split. On a CPU, use one thousand training examples and shorter texts. It takes about forty-five minutes. In the next lesson, we learn to evaluate deep models properly. See you there.
